Influenza Core Outcome Set · Delphi consensus project

FLU-CORE

Agreeing on what to measure — and how — in influenza clinical trials worldwide.

An international, multi-stakeholder consensus project developing a Core Outcome Set for influenza: the minimum set of outcomes that every flu trial should measure and report, chosen together by patients, carers, clinicians, researchers and policymakers.

Background & rationale

Influenza trials don't measure the same things

Influenza is highly prevalent, yet flu studies vary enormously in which outcomes they report and how they measure them. That heterogeneity makes results hard to compare, combine, or trust — fragmenting our understanding of which treatments actually work.

Inconsistent outcomes

Clinical trials use widely differing endpoints and measurement instruments, limiting meta-analysis and systematic review.

Patient voice missing

The outcomes that matter most to people with lived experience and their carers are too often left out of trial design.

✓

A shared minimum standard

A Core Outcome Set defines the small set of “core” outcomes that should be measured and reported in every influenza trial.

⤢

Comparable, combinable evidence

Consistency makes it far easier to pool results across studies — strengthening meta-analyses, reviews and guideline development.

◎

Built by everyone involved

Outcomes are selected by a broad coalition — patients, carers, clinicians, researchers, regulators and policymakers alike.

♥

Minimal risk, significant benefit

Participation is a series of optional online surveys and meetings, supporting better-designed trials and clearer clinical decisions.

The concept

From a long list of outcomes to an agreed core

FLU-CORE produces two complementary, consensus-built standards — first what to measure, then how to measure it.

COS Core Outcome Set

The what

An agreed, minimal set of the most critical outcomes that should be measured and reported in all influenza clinical trials — so the most important effects on people are never overlooked.

COMS Core Outcome Measurement Set

The how

For each core outcome, the valid, reliable and feasible measurement instrument(s) the field agrees should be used — assessed against COSMIN guidelines.

Two populations, two parallel sets

The protocol develops two separate Core Outcome Sets, run in parallel through the same rigorous process.

Track A Adults

Influenza in adults (≥18)

Lived-experience adults, family carers, and professionals with clinical, research, regulatory or policy expertise in adult influenza.

Track B Children

Influenza in children (0–17)

Young people (16+) with lived experience, carers of under-18s, and professionals working with influenza in children and young people.

Methodology

How consensus is reached

A systematic, inclusive sequence — combining evidence review, patient & public involvement, an open survey, and a modified online Delphi, finalised in a moderated consensus meeting.

Phase 1

Define the core outcomes

★ Result: Core Outcome Set (COS)
1

Scoping review

Mine published trials & registered protocols for every outcome reported — building one long list.

2

Expert review + PPIE

Specialists and patient/public partners consolidate and reword outcomes into a clear shortlist.

3

Open survey

Anyone affected by flu rates the shortlist worldwide, in multiple languages, informing the Delphi.

4

Delphi · Round 1

Panellists score each outcome and suggest additions.

AdultsChildren
Between rounds

Review new suggestions. Outcomes proposed by ≥5% of participants are assessed by investigators & the Steering Committee for inclusion in Round 2.

5

Delphi · Round 2

Panellists re-score the full list — now seeing their own Round 1 score and each stakeholder group's distribution.

AdultsChildren
6

Consensus meeting

A moderated virtual / hybrid meeting resolves outcomes that didn't meet thresholds — finalising the COS.

★ Core Outcome Set (COS) finalised — the agreed list of what to measure
Phase 2

Define how to measure them

★ Result: Core Outcome Measurement Set (COMS)
7

Map instruments

A literature review maps candidate measurement instruments to each agreed core outcome.

8

Expert review

Experts assess validity, reliability & feasibility (per COSMIN) and approve instruments for an expert Delphi.

9

Expert Delphi · R1 & R2

Participants score instruments per outcome over two anonymised rounds, recommending alternatives.

10

Consensus workshop

Final selection of the measurement instrument(s) for each core outcome.

Note

Additional Delphi rounds or meetings may be added depending on the complexity of the outcomes and instruments selected.

★ Core Outcome Measurement Set (COMS) finalised — then disseminated worldwide
Rating & consensus

How importance is scored — and what counts as agreement

Outcomes are rated on the GRADE 9-point scale. Pre-defined thresholds, applied across all stakeholder groups, decide what enters the core set.

The GRADE 9-point scale

Each outcome is rated 1–9, grouped into three bands of importance.

1–3
Not important
4–6
Important
7–9
Critical

In the open survey, participants are randomly assigned a 3-, 6- or 9-point scale — a built-in sub-study evaluating how rating-scale design affects responses. Only participants who rate at least 50% of items are included in the analysis.

Consensus thresholds

≥80%

Outcome included

Rated “critical” by ≥80% of participants in all stakeholder groups after Round 2.

≤50%

Outcome excluded

Rated “critical” by ≤50% across all stakeholder groups. Anything in between goes to the consensus meeting.

≥70%

Instrument included

A measurement instrument enters the COMS when ≥70% of voting participants rate it critically important.

Responses from participants employed by for-profit industry inform discussion but are excluded from the final consensus tally.

Who takes part

An inclusive, global coalition

Recruited openly through professional networks, the influenza literature, social media and the ISARIC website — by snowball and convenience sampling, across many countries and languages.

♥

Patients & carers

People with lived experience of influenza and the family members who cared for or advocated for them.

✚

Health professionals

Clinicians with expertise in treating or caring for people with influenza.

⚗

Researchers

Those who design, conduct, oversee or fund influenza research and clinical trials.

§

Policy & regulators

People developing policy or regulating influenza research, ensuring outcomes are decision-relevant.

Timeline

A 24-month consensus journey

An indicative sequence — participants may join throughout the study period as each phase runs.

1
Months 1–6

Evidence & shortlist

Scoping review, expert classification and PPIE refine the candidate outcomes.

2
Months 6–10

Open survey

Global, multilingual rating of the shortlist opens the process to all stakeholders.

3
Months 10–18

Delphi & consensus

Two Delphi rounds plus a moderated meeting finalise the Core Outcome Set.

4
Months 18–24

Instruments & sharing

Measurement instruments agreed and results disseminated worldwide.
